newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa overseas allowance to exceed 80,000 rand.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa overseas allowance to exceed 80,000 rand.

text.p: South Africa's Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Wednesday that individuals would be allowed to invest offshore "substantially" more than the 80,000 rand they will be permitted to use for overseas travel each year.
"It would have to be substantially more than (the 80,000 rand)...to distinguish between the travel allowance and the investment," Finance Minister Trevor Manuel told Reuters Financial Television.
He was speaking after his budget announcement which promised significant moves towards dismantling currency controls.
Manuel declined to give a precise figure for the individual offshore investment ceiling, but added he did not expect the changes to lead to a flood of money leaving the country.
"We don't see an enormous surge in the short-term," he said.
It would take until July 1 for the administrative procedures to be put in place, he added.
Asked if the allowance would be more than 100,000 rand, he said: "I would imagine that (but) I couldn't give you a ballpark figure now."

On privatisation, Manuel said he did not want to be drawn on overall privatisation revenues for 1997/8 given ongoing negotiations on the sale of a 30 percent stake in state-owned Telkom to a U.S.-Malaysia consortium.
"I think other privatisations may be affected by what happens in this our first huge privatisation," he said.
In his budget Manuel made provision only for 516 million rand in receipts from the sale of six radio stations.

He earlier estimated the budget deficit in the year to March 31, 1998, at four percent of gross domestic product. Manuel told RFTV this figure compared to a 5.4 percent deficit in 1996/7, which excluded extraordinary revenues.
In response to market concern that the spending and deficit targets would be realised, Manuel said: "It is going to be hard but I think that if nothing else we are stubborn enough to work at this."
Expenditure in 1997/8 is budgeted to rise 6.1 percent, substantially lower than the projected 8.5 percent inflation.
